userJob: Plan the narrow layout as a layout rather than as a consequence
problem: It stacks is what happens when nobody decided. The columns become rows in source order, the argument order is whatever the DOM happened to be, and a drawing scaled to a third of its width keeps annotation sized for the width it no longer has.
worksWhen: The page has more than one column, more than one drawing, or any element whose meaning depends on its proportions
avoidWhen: A single column of prose at every width, which should say exactly that once and stop
mechanism: Write what the layout IS at 375, at 768 and at 1440, in the page’s own terms. Name what is deliberately different at each. Then measure: if the leading elements sit in the same arrangement at 375 and 1440, the page was designed once and allowed to reflow.
risks: Reordering visually with grid or flex so the reading order and the focus order disagree
Scaling a measured drawing without redrawing its annotation, which produces a drawing nobody can read
mobileRules: The narrow view is a design, not a fallback. Decide its order rather than inheriting it.
A drawing that carries meaning owes its own annotation sizes at each width
accessibilityRules: The visual order and the focus order are the same order, or the difference is stated and defensible
Reflow at 320 CSS pixels and at 200 per cent zoom are the same requirement approached from two directions
genericnessNote: Naming the transformation does not prescribe one. Two pages with the same contract field can be entirely different pages.

userJob: Have every state a form can be in exist, be reachable, and be understood without colour
problem: Empty, loading, partial, error and success are written down as a requirement and built as an afterthought, so the empty state is a zero, the error is a red border with no message, and the success state is the form again with the fields cleared.
worksWhen: Anything the visitor types into, chooses from, or waits for
avoidWhen: A page with nothing to operate, which should say so rather than inventing a control
mechanism: Decide each state before implementation and say what changes and what carries it besides colour. Empty says what it will show rather than zero. Loading holds the shape of the answer so nothing jumps. Error sits on the field that caused it and names the value and the limit. Success is the thing the visitor came for, not a confirmation that a form was submitted.
risks: One error region at the top of the form, which is a summary and not an error on the field that caused it
A disabled submit button as the whole validation story, which tells a visitor nothing about what is wrong
mobileRules: An error message under a field must not be hidden behind the on-screen keyboard; scroll it into view
Do not rely on hover for anything a state depends on
accessibilityRules: The message is programmatically associated with its field, and the field is marked invalid
A state change is announced once, and not on every keystroke
Colour alone is not a state: a border that thickens, a mark, or a weight change carries it too
genericnessNote: These are behaviours rather than appearances. Two forms that both do this look nothing alike.

userJob: Give the page a shell that says who this is, where they are, and one thing to do
problem: Navigation is either absent, on the theory that a single page does not need it, or it is a full site menu on a page with three sections. The cleanest correlation in this repository’s own cold builds was this one: the rejected pages had one anchor each, the skip link, and no nav and no footer between them.
worksWhen: Every page, including the ones that are one screen long
avoidWhen: Never entirely, though the answer can be four anchors and a footer rather than a menu
mechanism: Decide what the shell is: who this is, where the reader is, and one thing they can do. Anchors to the page’s own sections count. A footer with the real address, the real hours and the real telephone number is a shell.
risks: A menu that wraps three and one at 375, which reads as a missing item rather than as a wrap
A sticky header that eats a quarter of a small screen
mobileRules: A wrapped menu is set deliberately, two by two or one per line, rather than left to wrap
The skip link is the first focusable thing and is visible when focused
accessibilityRules: The current section is marked, not only coloured
A menu that opens is a disclosure with a name, an expanded state, and a way back out on the keyboard
genericnessNote: A logo left, four links right and one button far right is the most reproduced shell there is. What is in the shell is what makes it this page’s.

userJob: Show a set of numbers so the difference between them is visible without depending on hue
problem: A chart is given a categorical palette, and the difference between two series is a difference between two colours. For a reader who cannot tell those two apart, the chart has one series.
worksWhen: Anything with more than one series, more than one category, or a scale
avoidWhen: A single value, which is a number and should be set as one
mechanism: Say how many series there are and whether the ordering is categorical, sequential or diverging, then say what carries the difference when colour does not: position, shape, hatch, thickness, or a direct label on the line. Colour is the last thing added, not the first.
risks: A sequential scale built from a categorical palette, so equal steps in the data are unequal steps in the eye
More series than a reader can hold, which is a chart that needs to be two charts
mobileRules: A chart that has to be scrolled sideways is announced as scrollable and is reachable by keyboard
Direct labels beat a legend at 375, where a legend costs a third of the screen
accessibilityRules: The chart has a text alternative that carries the finding, not a description of the shape
Non-text contrast applies to the parts of a graphic needed to understand it
genericnessNote: The default chart palette of whatever library is installed is the genericness risk here, and it is a large one.

userJob: Use marks that belong to this subject rather than to the icon set that was installed
problem: An icon library is added and every section gets an icon, all at the same weight, all from the same hand, none from this subject. Three feature cards with a rocket, a shield and a lightning bolt is the most reproduced arrangement on the internet.
worksWhen: The page has a repeated set of things that genuinely need identifying at a glance: tools, states, materials, controls
avoidWhen: Decorating a heading. An icon next to a section title is almost always the library speaking rather than the subject.
mechanism: Decide the system first: one stroke weight, one corner treatment, one grid, one metaphor family, drawn from the subject’s own world. Then draw only the marks the page needs. A system of four drawn marks beats a set of two hundred borrowed ones.
risks: Mixing two libraries, which shows immediately in stroke weight and corner radius
An icon carrying meaning with no text beside it
mobileRules: An icon-only control still owes a 44px target and an accessible name
accessibilityRules: Decorative marks are hidden from assistive technology; meaningful ones have names
An icon that carries meaning owes 3:1 against its ground
genericnessNote: This is the single most reliable tell of a generated page. If the marks came from a library, the page could be about anything.
